items.title: The Trump Administration Wanted Her Expertise, Just Not Her
items.description: Editor's Note: Read Julia Curlee’s full essay here . Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts When Julia Curlee was a kid growing up in Hawaii, she dreamed of becoming an intelligence officer. In 2007, when she took her oath standing on the marble CIA seal, she achieved that goal. But she had another childhood dream too: She’d always had “an unshakable belief that I should have been born a woman.” In 2013, Julia Curlee became the first CIA officer to transition openly and keep serving the agency. She felt more effective at her job living as the person she always believed she was— and years ago wrote about her experience under a pseudonym in The Atlantic. Her performance proved her effectiveness: She became the daily intelligence briefer for Vice President Pence during the first Trump administration and a director on the National Security Council in both the Biden administration and the second Trump term. Less than 70 days after the president returned to office in 2025, Julia was fired from the White House without explanation. She returned to the CIA and, over time, began to feel a lack of support at the agency in an administration that was openly hostile to transgender people. Julia left her dream job with the federal government earlier this year. This week, she is telling her full story for the first time—in an Atlantic essay she wrote and in a conversation with Radio Atlantic . The following is a transcript of the episode: Julia Curlee: After everything I had been through with my service to the former vice president, my briefing for this president in the first term, and my war zones, my 20 years, all of it, “Be discreet” meant We need you. We need your service. But we don’t want anyone to know you are here . Adam Harris: As a high-level CIA officer, Julia Curlee had the ear of one of the most powerful politicians in America: the vice president of the United States. He relied on her to let him know what was going on in the world each day. She held prominent intelligence positions during the last three administrations: Trump 1, Biden, and Trump 2. She is also a transgender woman. For a long time, Julia had two dreams: to be a CIA officer and to be her authentic self. She realized the first in 2007, when she took the oath on the agency seal; the second in 2013, when she transitioned. She made a promise when she did: never to hide who she was. Yet in 2017, she wrote two stories for The Atlantic under a pseudonym. She wrote about her experience; she wrote about what it meant for the intelligence community to accept people like her. The agency used it to help recruit on college campuses. Julia was using the discretion that came naturally for a CIA officer. Now, after being pushed out of the White House and leaving an agency where she no longer felt supported, Julia is telling the rest of the story as herself. I’m Adam Harris. This is Radio Atlantic , and today: a conversation with Julia Curlee. Let’s get to questions. Julia, welcome to the show. Julia Curlee: Thank you, Adam. Thanks for having me. Harris: Absolutely. So Julia, you served the United States for more than 20 years in intelligence positions. What was it that drew you to public service? Curlee: Well, I grew up a barefoot kid in Hawaii, and I always wanted to see what was over the horizon and see the world and all that. And then, at some young, impressionable age, I was ambushed by The Hunt for Red October and the analyst as hero, getting to save the day. And, I don’t know, it sort of came out of nowhere and it sort of bubbled up in my life. And my parents definitely instilled in me a desire to serve our country, and intelligence just caught something in me and I wanted to be a part of it. Harris: When you joined, was it everything you imagined? Curlee: Oh, many more late nights and long PowerPoint-presentation sessions. Harris: So not quite like the movie? Curlee : Not so much, yeah. I didn’t call in many drone strikes on my way to the PowerPoint presentation that you would sometimes see in the movies. Did not repel off a helicopter into a submarine too many times. But it was an amazing and wonderful career. I got to travel to 35 countries. I briefed several presidents. It was just all I wanted to do, and I desperately wish I was doing that now. It’s the only thing I ever wanted to do and it was the only plan I ever had. Harris: And today you’re writing in the pages of The Atlantic , telling your story for the first time under your own name. Why now? Curlee: Well the institutions that I served through my adult life are under assault. The ability of officers to speak truth to power, to inform policy making so that they make the best decisions on behalf of the United States—that is being eviscerated. And the officers who deliver that, who spend their lives learning about foreign countries, learning how to systematically understand multiple sources of intelligence, convey uncertainty—all of that is being destroyed by an administration that wants to both cherry-pick the intelligence to only receive what they want to hear, and to punish the officers who have the courage to speak that truth to them, to do their jobs and to live up to the values that we inculcate in all of our officers. And so the only way to do that was to leave and to begin to tell my story. I also felt like I needed to tell the other part of my story, which has nothing to do with my substantive experience in the world, and that’s being a trans person. And I know that the sustained assault on people like me is a part of a broader campaign to try to define who gets to be in public spaces, who gets to have positions of honor. Harris: I want to talk about that service and about your transition while you were in the service. You transitioned in 2013, and did you have concerns when you were transitioning? What was that first day going into the office like? Curlee: Well, it was the most terrifying day of my life. And that was in the wake of several war-zone assignments and being rocketed, and I didn’t know whether it would be the last day. You know, as I already said, I’d always dreamed since I was a kid of being an intelligence officer. The other dream that I’d always had that was unexplainable was just an unshakable belief that I should have been more born a woman. I didn’t know where it came from. It just was always lurking in the background. And over time in my life, it became this just unshakable darkness that clouded out everything else. And finally, I came to the conclusion I had to transition. The only problem, of course, is that there were no trans people. The last time someone at CIA had tried to transition had been decades before, and it had been terrible. The person had been driven out of the organization, in a hostile workplace, and management had not been supportive. And so I contacted the LGBT group to say, Hey, I’m here. I’m here to meet other people and get some help . And they said, Congratulations, but you’re the only one . And that is what led me in 2017 to write in pseudonym in The Atlantic under the name Jenny Hall. And it was an opportunity to get the word out that people like me are a part of our national security, that we’re patriots, that we want to serve, that we don’t want any special rights. We just want what everyone else has. And so I was very happy to get to do that. And in the years following that, CIA actually used those articles on college campuses to recruit people. And I was very proud of that, but I was also very, very happy to disappear back into my day job, in the work. And so, you know, in short, my transition in those years was a big “nothing significant to report,” in the lexicon of my profession, and that was the best possible outcome. Harris: So when you talk about the work, this is 2017; the first Trump administration has just begun. What were your concerns? Did you have concerns ahead of that first Trump administration about their policies, or the platform, regarding transgender people? Curlee: You know, going into that term, it really hadn’t been in the political realm very much. I mean, it honestly wasn’t a big issue. It only really became, in my consciousness anyway, a big political issue when the president, the first time, banned trans people in the military, which was a shock, because for a lot of us it was a rock-solid belief that progress is linear, that things you gained might slow down, but, you know, the long arc, and that things would get better. And this was a case of it regressing in a significant way. And I knew several trans intelligence officers who were in uniform who were doing the same job that I was doing at CIA, and they were being told that by being honest, by which the previous administration had told them they could be, that they would be thrown out and that their careers would be destroyed just for being themselves. And so I also wrote about that to try to make the case in a good-faith way to our leaders that this was the wrong decision and that it would hurt our national security. Harris: So you gave the president’s daily brief during that first Trump administration. Can you tell us what it means to do that job and what all it entails? Curlee: Yeah, so as a baby analyst, you imagine yourself being that briefer in the room with the commander in chief or briefing on Air Force One. It was the thing that most of us aspired to at the end of a long career. And initially I was assigned to the deputy national security adviser in the White House. And boy, it was like cramming for a final exam every morning from midnight to 5 a.m. or so. And then at some point there, you’re whisked downtown and you come to the White House when it’s pitch black and you check in with the Situation Room, and you’ve got these pieces that you’ve been studying. And so I would get to the White House and I would find my—I’d be the first person that would see my policy customer when they came in the door in the West Wing, the deputy national security adviser, at first, and I would be in there for 15, 20, 30, 40, 50 minutes, and it would be 20 questions, and it would be firing things at me and asking me to follow up with taskings. And it was just exhilarating for a person that was a news junkie who wants to be plugged into the information universe, just wanting to be available to help these policy makers make good decisions. And I did that for two years in total for the Trump administration for the first term. Harris: And so, while you’re in the Trump administration, you begin giving the president’s daily briefing, and you begin giving that briefing to Vice President Mike Pence. What was the experience of first meeting him like? Curlee: Yeah, so I’d been in the PDB for a few months, and it was wonderful. And as much as I loved roaming the West Wing of the White House before dawn and no one caring apparently that a trans woman was serving the highest levels of the Trump administration, my boss walked into my office one day and said, you know, Julia, what would you think about briefing the vice president? And I looked up at her and I said, This vice president? And she said, Yeah, I think you’d be the right pick for this. And I took her word for it. And so, the first time I was standing in the driveway at the Naval Observatory when there he was, unmistakably, with his silver-white hair, and he turns to his outgoing briefer and said, You’re gonna abandon me with her? And it was his dad-joke humor, and there I was, and it was just me and Mike Pence. And I discovered that he was an excellent intelligence customer. He took the book, he took the briefing almost every day, religiously. He took rapid notes and would be firing questions at me. And he really impressed me with how seriously he was taking the job of being this consumer of intelligence, this massive, multibillion-dollar apparatus we’ve built out to help our leaders make better decisions. And he was using it as I would have hoped he would. And in a broader administration where that was not always the case, I really felt like I could really do good, and support him as he participated in these policy conversations. And it was a real pleasure. It was truly the thing that I had been training and and wanting to do since I’d been a kid. It was like the experience that I dreamed of. Harris: Yeah, so he was really relying on you for your expertise? Curlee: Yeah, I mean, I would be one of the first people he would see in the morning. It has been described to me that a PDB briefer is—part of your job is, like, helping to filter the world so that a policy maker whose most precious commodity is time can know what are the really big issues to focus on. And I would play that part in his day, in focusing him on the key events happening in one part of the world versus another, teeing up information so that I would know what policy-making meetings he was going into or heading on a foreign trip, and I would be trying to anticipate his needs, and then when he asked a question, ensure that it was rapidly answered as quickly as possible. And so getting to travel with him around the world, getting to be a part of the team that follows the vice president, was truly an amazing privilege. And for all of the fears and my own trepidations—I wasn’t ignorant of his public persona. It truly was a great experience, and I got to see our government operating as it should. Harris: There’s probably some dissonance there, right, between that public persona and the private persona? How do you square the difference between the public policy and and the person who you engaged with on a regular basis? Curlee: I don’t know, and I don’t want to suggest that I know his personal views. What I know is what I experienced. I experienced being treated with great respect, being treated as a serious professional, being trusted. When my tour was over, he asked me to extend. So that was a conversation to have with my wife. But I had been raised in a CIA that had trained into us that we serve regardless of who sits in the Oval Office, that we are nonpartisan civil servants who will support them with the best information possible. And he was the vice president and needed the best information possible. And so what I would do is I would put that to the side. It was the fulfillment of what I had always wanted to do, and there were moments like when my tour was finally coming to an end and he invited my family to the White House, and he took my mother’s hand—and this is my mother who had had a really hard time with my transition years before—and Mike Pence took my mother’s hand and says, You must be very proud of your daughter . And I’m sitting there watching this and I’m thinking, We’ve arrived . There’s no more battles left to be won . I mean, it’s not, that wasn’t true, but it just felt like the two dreams that I’d had since I was a kid, which I had always felt were just completely incompatible. Harris: You write about the moment that the vice president certified the election and how there was a certain sort of kinship between the two of you around that service, right? That you mentioned the, sort of, bargain, right? The exact quote was, “That was the bargain: service before politics, country before self.” Can you tell me about that moment? What that moment signified for you? Curlee: So, this was a few days after January 6 and I had been done briefing him for several months at that point. And he brought us all together, and we were in his West Wing office just down the hall from the Oval, and we went around talking about what serving in this role had meant to us. And I told him that moment, when he had prioritized the country, when he had certified the victory of his opponent in the election, that I was never more proud to have served as his briefer. And he, you know, he took my hand; we shook hands, and he said that meant a lot to him. And that is what the bargain meant to me, was the fact that despite our almost certain profound differences of views on many subjects, we could put that aside and treat each other with dignity and do what was right, regardless of our politics and the political cost. And it was a very special moment for me and everybody who was there. Harris: So, after four years of the Biden administration, the Trump administration comes back for a second time, and people begin to decide whether they should stay or go. So what advice were you getting about what you should do? Curlee: It was fairly uniform that we should all leave. So during the campaign I had been serving at the White House; I served for about 20 months in the Biden administration as a director for intelligence programs in the NSC. And all throughout that period, it was wall-to-wall TV. I remember standing in the sit room, looking up at one of the many screens and watching these scary images of people like me and hundreds of millions of dollars being poured to create this caricature that somehow trans people were a threat to America and tar the Democratic candidate with association with these scary people. And I’m watching this and in horror that I’m witnessing on the TV the same kind of dehumanization that I’d written PDBs about in my career. And so, but, despite all of that, despite the warnings from our leadership that they were very afraid for us, that we would be targeted, that it would destroy our careers, that the online mob would be summoned against us—despite all of that, I was the trans woman that briefed Mike Pence. I believed fiercely in the idea of nonpartisan civil service to whoever is the president. And I was not going to walk away from this task that I had been given to help with the peaceful transfer of power of an administration. And so, the only person in the whole White House, I have to say, who asked us to stay was the president. And I believed it, that was the right decision. And I still believe it still. But almost everyone that decided to do that has paid a price in some form or another. And so when the politicals departed, about a week out from the turn of administration, I was asked to serve as the acting senior director for intelligence programs. And so I was there when the new team arrived on Inauguration Day. I was there in the West Wing as people were still finding their offices, as people were moving in the furniture and moving in the new furniture, when the vice president arrived and saw his office for the first time. I was there to help the new administration get off the ground. And I did. And for day after day, we did that until the third day, when the administration, while I was briefing the deputy national security adviser, summoned 160 NSE detailees from departments and agencies to a group call and told them they had 15 minutes to get off the compound. I walked out of my briefing with a handful of taskings that I knew I needed to get to the intelligence community as quickly as possible. And my assistant intercepts me on West Exec, the road between the White House and the EEOB, where my office was, and says, Everyone’s fired except for you . And I was in shock at the recklessness and the callousness of it. And so over the next several days, it was a mess. And so for the next 69 days, I and the few people from my team that I could bring back served until one day on a Saturday, I’m down in Roanoke, Virginia, with my family, and I get a phone call that says that my tour is over. The chief of staff called. I can’t give you a reason why. You’re gone. You’ll be sent back to CIA. But if you don’t mind, we’d still like you to come in on Monday . Harris: So you were removed from your position and asked to come back in. Curlee: Yeah, in the same phone call, you know, fired on Saturday but needed on Monday. But I was warned in that call to be discreet. And I still didn’t understand what was happening until I got off the phone and my iPhone was was bombarded with friend after friend after friend forwarding me a tweet that said, that announced to the world, that there was a trans Biden holdover who hates President Trump in the intelligence directorate, and please give me this person’s name so that I can out them to the world. And I was terrified of what that would mean for me and my family. But Monday came and I came to work anyway. And I served for another three days to help finish off an important budget item that I had been working on, to turn over a portfolio that I had managed at that point for almost two years, and it was that third night, my last day there, that a list of enemies within the administration was given to the president. And it was yet another purge of people with decades of experience, including my boss at the time. And, you know, as I was leaving the White House for that last time, with my little box of mementos from two years of serving at the White House, you know, this dream come true, it really hit me what “Be discreet” meant in that point, after everything I had been through with my service to the former vice president, my briefing for this president in the first term, and my war zones, my 20 years, all of it, “Be discreet” meant We need you. We need your service. But we don’t want anyone to know you are here. And that has stuck with me ever since, and why I have to tell my story, because they’ve taken from me my calling. I can no longer serve. I couldn’t use the bathroom. When I was at the White House, I had to cross the street to coffee shops across Pennsylvania Avenue in order to just get through the day. And the same restrictions followed me back to CIA. And the constant fear of being fired for being who I am just—I couldn’t continue. But the one thing I can’t allow for me is for the fact that what has happened has already happened. It can’t be undone. And so telling my story is a part of putting that on the record, that someone like me can serve in the White House, can brief a president, can serve honorably, and loves their country. And so I had to tell this story. Harris: You mentioned the list of enemies landing on Trump’s desk, and the tweet hunting for the transgender intelligence person in the White House. That tweet and the list came from Laura Loomer, who is a far-right provocateur. If she never posted that tweet, if that list had never gone out, do you think that you might still be in the White House? Curlee: I think I probably would have reached my limit at some point in terms of my family, and it would have been time for someone else to come. But I fully intended to keep serving, and at the time it was funny. In that same conversation that I was in with the deputy national security adviser, briefing him on some very sensitive, important programs, he asked me when my tour was over, and I said, Well, sir, it’s been—it’ll be two years and just in a couple months, and , you know, I gotta get home and I’ve got a family . And he said, Hmm, June. I don’t think that’s gonna work for us . And so, I was already starting to think how I was gonna have this conversation again. But I wanted to keep serving, and keep serving at CIA. That was my only plan, and I’m just sad that it became impossible. Harris: I want to home in on your expertise. You’ve said that what Americans should be concerned about is this wider assault on expertise in this administration, and especially in the intelligence community. So are we already seeing the consequences of that assault on expertise and elimination of expertise? Curlee: I’m regretting to say we are, and it’s all around us in the evidence of disastrous policies. But to back up a second, you know, the same assault on trans officers, on other minorities, was accompanied by a parallel attack on the ability of our officers to speak truth to power. So, one of the things that happened early in the new administration was I was asked to send a tasking to the intelligence community on the status of this group Tren de Aragua, which was a Venezuelan street gang. And the tasking was whether the Maduro government had ordered this group to invade the United States, which is the predicate for invoking the Alien Enemies Act almost verbatim, and I tasked it out to the National Intelligence Council, where the chairman of the NIC, which is the most senior analytic body in the intelligence community, dutifully wrote an excellent assessment that reflected the consensus position of the intelligence community. And he and his deputy, when they delivered the product, which did not accord with what the administration wanted to hear, were told that they should rethink their assessment. And when they refused, they were ordered out of the building. And publicly firing one of the most esteemed officers in the intelligence community and their deputy for living up to the values that we inculcate in every young officer was a devastating blow to the whole organization. And it has had ripple effects all through. And it is just further attacks on officers for assessments that they wrote a decade ago, because they don’t conform with what the president wants to hear, has taught this generation now of officers that your clearance can be revoked with a phone call if you say the wrong thing. And so a muzzle has been put on an organization that is vital to our national interest. And when you wed that with the destruction of the National Security Council as a policy-coordinating body, which I got to witness firsthand through the purges that unfolded through the first few months of the administration, you’ve lost the very venue in which those concerns and experts and expertise can be delivered to help the president make good decisions. And so it’s not surprising when disastrous outcomes ensue. So, just for the example, when the country was marching to war in Iran, America launched a full suite of airstrikes showing that the U.S. military is the finest fighting force in the world. And at the same time, the State Department somehow hadn’t planned for the evacuation of half a million Americans and diplomats and officers and their dependents in a war we started. In any competent administration, regardless of the wisdom of the effort, there would have been a plan. And there would have been a plan to deal with the fact that the Iranians were going to close the Strait of Hormuz. There would have been briefings that would have made clear to the president that decapitating the leadership and killing the supreme leader would not immediately lead to the Iranians surrendering. All of these things are what the intelligence community and the National Security Council should exist to do, to head off these things, to ensure that things that are foreseeable and have been foreseen in multiple public war games for decades about the Iranians would have been delivered and provided context for the administration to make a sound decision or at least plan. And none of it happened. And as a result, we’re in this debacle where there’s no clear road out, where all the choices are terrible. And we’re looking at ending the conflict in a worse position than when we begun. And there’s, I think there’s a word for that, and it’s called losing a war . And this is a direct result of a climate of fear that the administration has instilled on a workforce that it somehow sees as the enemy within rather than the civil servants who have given their professional lives to helping the country. And we’re all paying for it. Harris: You wrote that your grandfather told you “Work hard; don’t complain; and the country will take care of you.” Do you still think the country is taking care of you? Curlee: No, no. It’s hard to feel the sense of betrayal, a bit. And it’s not just me; it’s all of the people who devoted themselves to this ideal of nonpartisan public service, who have been callously thrown away. I’ve got many friends who are transgender in the military, who have faced ruinous financial and life circumstances and had something so important to their identities taken away from them for no reason at all, other than just animus for who some people are. And that’s why I titled the piece “The Wrong Kind of American,” because it really is that. It is a decision to treat some Americans as not worthy of a full life, of positions of honor, and to treat them as if they’re some sort of threat to society. And it feels as if we’ve just turned our back on the most fundamental ideal that we try to teach everyone, which is that we can rise as far as our talents take us in this country. And that’s a terrible thing. You know, nine years ago I closed my piece in The Atlantic saying trans kids should know that CIA is always recruiting , because I wanted them to know that there was this amazing life that they could have, that there were some people like them who got to do that, and now I could not in good conscience advise any LGBT American to apply to work at CIA. And that is awful. That is un-American, and I regret saying it, but it’s just true. And I hope that in the coming years that will change and we’ll do what’s right, and we’ll look back at this period in our history with shame and we’ll learn from it. Harris: Julia, thank you so much for sharing your story and for joining me on the show today. Curlee: Thank you. It was a privilege. Harris: That’s all for today’s show. This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Mike Pesoli and edited by Claudine Ebeid. It was engineered by Miguel Carrascal and has original music by Rob Smierciak. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic Audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor. If you like what you saw here, new episodes of Radio Atlantic drop every Monday and Thursday. You can subscribe on The Atlantic ’s YouTube page, on Apple or Spotify, or wherever it is you get your podcasts. And if you want to support this work and the work of my colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at theatlantic.com/listener. Until next time, I’m Adam Harris.

items.title: Mahama announces new strategy to keep galamseyers out of reclaimed forest reserves
items.description: President John Mahama says the government has adopted a new strategy to prevent illegal miners from returning to forest reserves after they have been cleared of galamsey activities. Under the new approach, military detachments will remain in reclaimed forest reserves to protect them from renewed encroachment, he said. President Mahama explained that the decision followed the failure of the previous approach, under which cleared forest reserves were handed back to the Forestry Commission. Speaking during his tour of the Upper East Region, he said illegal miners had repeatedly returned to some reserves after the military and other enforcement teams had cleared them. “We are working; NAIMOS is working very hard. We’ve seized excavators, we’ve seized Changfan machines, and you drive them out of this area, they run to this other area. But we are making progress,” he said. President Mahama said the government had so far cleared as many as possible of the nearly 49 forest reserves that had been invaded by illegal miners. He said the government had, however, realised that simply handing the cleared reserves back to the Forestry Commission was not enough to prevent renewed illegal mining. “Before, what we did was when we cleared, we handed over to the Forestry Services Commission. But they don’t fear the Forest Service; they go and drive the forest guards out, and they go back into the mine. And so now we put a military detachment,” he said. Under the new arrangement, he said, soldiers would remain in the reserves after the illegal miners had been removed. “After we’ve cleared the forest reserve, we leave a military detachment there. And that means we have to spend more money. One, you must feed the soldiers; you must provide them with the logistics to continue to stay there in the forest,” President Mahama said. Despite the additional cost, the President said his government would remain committed to the fight against illegal mining. “But we will not give up; we will continue the fight against illegal mining,” he said. Government targets formalisation of mining While stressing the need to curb illegal mining, President Mahama said the government also recognised the potential of the mining sector to create jobs for young people in the Upper East Region and elsewhere. He said the government’s objective was to formalise mining activities to improve regulation and create sustainable employment opportunities. “Upper East has good potential, and mining can create jobs, but we need to make sure that these are formalised mines so that they can employ our young people to operate,” he said. READ ALSO : Cedi is ‘long overdue for a refresh’ – Mahama – MyJoyOnline President Mahama cited the opening of Cardinal Mine in the region as an example of how formal mining operations could contribute to job creation. He also pointed to the Black Volta mine development in the Upper West Region as another example of the potential for properly regulated mining to create employment. “In Upper West, they have the Black Volta mine development coming up. There are several other areas that we can see the potential for proper mining so that it can produce more jobs for our young people,” he said. He stressed that the government’s goal was to formalise mining and establish greater control over the sector rather than allow unregulated and scattered illegal mining activities to continue. “Our target is to formalise the mining activity so that we have greater control over it than the current scattered illegal mining that takes place,” President Mahama said. Mahama distinguishes Upper East mining from forest destruction President Mahama also drew a distinction between mining activities in the Upper East Region and the environmental damage associated with illegal mining in forested areas in southern Ghana. According to him, much of the gold in the Upper East Region is found in rock formations, which means mining there does not cause the same level of environmental destruction associated with mining in forest reserves in the south. “The advantage with the Upper East Region is that most of the places where the gold is found are found in rock. And so it does not create the kind of environmental destruction that we see in the south,” he said. He explained that mining in such areas involves blasting rock and processing it to extract the gold. “The gold is found in rock, and so they blast the rock, and they process it and take the gold out,” he said. President Mahama said this meant the region did not experience the same extent of environmental devastation seen in forest reserves in southern Ghana. “And so it doesn’t create the same extent of devastation that we’re seeing in the forest in the south. And so that’s a fortunate thing,” he said. The government’s new strategy therefore represents a shift from simply removing illegal miners from forest reserves to maintaining a security presence in reclaimed areas to prevent their return, while pursuing the formalisation of mining activities outside protected areas.

items.title: Tribunal de Dixinn : Bella Bah nie les faits qui lui sont reprochés et regrette l’extrapolation de sa publication
items.description: Le procès de l’activiste Bella Bah, entrepreneur et fondateur d’école, s’est ouvert ce lundi 17 août 2026 devant le Tribunal de première instance de Dixinn, siégeant en audience correctionnelle. Il est poursuivi pour des faits « d’injure et diffamation par le biais d’un système d’information » au préjudice d’Elhadj Mamadou Saliou Camara. À l’ouverture de l’audience, le président du tribunal a appelé la partie civile, Elhadj Mamadou Saliou Camara, qui n’était toutefois pas présente dans la salle. Interrogé par le tribunal sur les circonstances de son arrestation, Bella Bah, qui s’est présenté comme entrepreneur, fondateur d’école et activiste, a déclaré qu’il n’avait pas été arrêté, mais plutôt « kidnappé à son école ». Selon lui, le samedi 8 août 2026, un pick-up de la gendarmerie est arrivé à son école alors qu’il s’y trouvait pour travailler. Un gendarme en civil se serait introduit dans son bureau et lui aurait demandé de le suivre. Bella Bah affirme avoir demandé le motif de cette démarche ainsi que l’autorisation de joindre son épouse et son avocat. Il affirme que les agents ont récupéré son téléphone de force avant de l’emmener à la gendarmerie. Il dit également avoir été entendu durant la nuit, en l’absence de son avocat, « de 22 heures jusqu’aux environs de 3 heures ». Interrogé sur les motivations de sa publication, Bella Bah a déclaré : « Je n’ai jamais eu l’intention d’injurier. » Il a expliqué qu’en tant qu’activiste, il apprécie « quand on fait du bien », mais qu’il critique et alerte lorsqu’il estime qu’une chose « n’est pas bien ». Concernant la publication au cœur de la procédure, Bella Bah nie avoir directement visé une personne ou avoir su que ses propos seraient associés à Elhadj Mamadou Saliou Camara. Il a également estimé que le discours auquel faisait référence sa publication « n’est pas le discours d’un religieux ». Face au procureur, le prévenu a nié avoir injurié Elhadj Mamadou Saliou Camara ou avoir eu l’intention de le faire. Il a toutefois reconnu l’avoir critiqué. Lorsque le procureur lui a demandé à qui il faisait référence en employant, dans son message, les termes « manipulateur » et « corrompu », Bella Bah est resté ferme : « Je n’ai pas de réponse à cette question. » Invité à définir les termes au centre des débats, il a expliqué qu’une personne malhonnête est « quelqu’un qui n’est pas honnête », qu’un manipulateur est « quelqu’un qui manipule pour arriver à ses fins » et qu’un corrompu est « quelqu’un qui effectue de la corruption ». Le procureur lui a alors demandé s’il disposait de preuves établissant qu’Elhadj Mamadou Saliou Camara était corrompu. Bella Bah a répondu : « Je n’ai pas dit qu’Elhadj Mamadou Saliou Camara est corrompu. » Répondant ensuite aux questions de ses avocats, Bella Bah a exprimé « un sentiment de regret par rapport à l’extrapolation » faite de sa publication. Il a indiqué que, s’il avait su que ses propos allaient donner lieu à de telles interprétations, il ne les aurait pas publiés. À la question de savoir s’il demandait pardon devant le tribunal, il a répondu : « Je n’ai pas de réponse à cette question. » Enfin, interrogé sur son intention de reproduire à l’avenir un commentaire similaire, Bella Bah a répondu par la négative. Il a toutefois contesté les conditions de son interpellation et de sa détention, affirmant notamment avoir été privé de nourriture et d’eau pendant quatre jours et avoir vu son délai de garde à vue renouvelé à deux reprises. « Maître, on devrait tout simplement me faire une convocation. Mais vous imaginez, j’ai été privé de nourriture et d’eau pendant quatre jours. Ils ont renouvelé deux fois mon délai de garde à vue. Ils m’ont placé en détention avec des condamnés, des gens qui ont fait braquage… », a-t-il déclaré face à l’une des questions de sa défense. Mamadou Yaya BARRY L’article Tribunal de Dixinn : Bella Bah nie les faits qui lui sont reprochés et regrette l’extrapolation de sa publication est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Philip Nai: KFC Ghana and the Gh¢15 promotion; Where does corporate responsibility begin?
items.description: I have spent almost two decades working across media, communications, public relations, brand strategy and production. As a Chartered Brand Management Professional, I understand the importance of building brands that attract attention, create consumer excitement and deliver commercial results. But strong brands are not built on visibility alone. They are also built on trust, responsibility and how an organisation responds when things go wrong. I am also a student of the law, and that perspective has increasingly sharpened my interest in the relationship between business decisions, public responsibility and legal accountability. That is the lens through which I am examining the events surrounding KFC Ghana’s GH¢15 anniversary promotion. I am writing as a media and communications professional, a Chartered Brand Management Professional and a student of the law, asking a straightforward question: When a commercial promotion creates a foreseeable public safety risk, where does the responsibility of the company begin, and where does it end? That question deserves a serious conversation. This Is Bigger Than a Cheap Meal There is nothing inherently wrong with a company offering an attractive promotion. In fact, from a marketing perspective, KFC’s GH¢15 anniversary offer was a powerful proposition. A meal at that price, particularly in the current economic environment, was always likely to generate significant consumer interest. And therein lies the first important issue. The success of the marketing campaign should have triggered an equally serious conversation about risk. When a company deliberately creates a promotion capable of attracting unusually large numbers of people to physical locations within a limited period, crowd management cannot be treated as an afterthought. It becomes part of the operational responsibility of the campaign. The question therefore is not whether customers were excited. They clearly were. The question is whether the company reasonably anticipated the level of demand and whether adequate measures were put in place to protect customers, staff and property. That is where the legal conversation begins. Foreseeability Matters Ghanaian courts have long recognised the principles of negligence. Broadly speaking, a claimant must establish that a duty of care existed, that the duty was breached, that the breach caused damage and that the damage is legally attributable to that breach. That framework is important here. A customer does not become a legal stranger simply because a promotion has attracted more people than expected. If a business invites the public onto its premises, the circumstances surrounding that invitation matter. And when the business itself designs, advertises and executes a promotion capable of generating exceptional footfall, the issue of foreseeable risk becomes difficult to ignore. The courts would ultimately have to examine the specific facts. How many people were expected? What crowd-control measures were planned? Were security personnel properly briefed? Were entry and exit points adequate? Were barriers or controlled access systems considered? Was the promotion structured in a way that could have reduced congestion? What happened when management realised that the crowd had exceeded the branch’s ability to safely manage it? These questions are more important than simply asking whether customers “misbehaved”. The Security Question Perhaps the most troubling aspect of the incident is the conduct attributed to some security personnel. There is a fundamental difference between crowd control and unlawful physical force. Security officers may have legitimate responsibilities to protect people and property and to restore order. But the authority to manage a crowd does not automatically become permission to use excessive or unlawful force. If a customer was unlawfully assaulted by a security officer, that person may potentially have a claim in tort, depending on the evidence and circumstances. The more complicated question is whether KFC itself could be held responsible. That would depend on several factors, including the relationship between KFC and the security personnel, whether the guards were employees or engaged through an external security company, what they were instructed to do, and whether the alleged conduct occurred within the scope of their assigned functions. The principle of vicarious liability can, in appropriate circumstances, make an employer responsible for wrongful conduct committed by an employee in the course of employment. That means a company cannot automatically wash its hands of conduct simply because it was carried out by an individual employee or security officer. But again, the facts matter. We should allow an investigation to establish exactly what happened. There Is Also a Statutory Safety Question Ghana has legislation dealing with safety in workplaces and commercial premises. The Factories, Offices and Shops Act, 1970 (Act 328), for example, contains provisions concerning the safety of workplaces and the responsibilities of occupiers. The legislation gives inspectors powers to address dangerous conditions and practices where there is a risk of bodily injury. That raises legitimate questions about the circumstances surrounding the KFC promotion. Were the relevant safety requirements satisfied? Was the expected volume of customers considered? Were adequate emergency procedures in place? Were security arrangements appropriate for the anticipated crowd? Were there mechanisms to control entry and exit? Were incidents properly documented? These are not questions for social media to answer. They are questions for the appropriate authorities to investigate. But Let Us Also Be Fair to KFC Accountability does not mean assuming guilt. That distinction is important. A large crowd does not automatically establish negligence. A damaged door does not, by itself, prove liability. A video showing a security officer using force does not, without further evidence, establish every element of a legal claim against KFC. The law requires evidence. It requires us to establish what happened, who did what, what duty existed, whether that duty was breached and whether the alleged breach caused legally recognised harm. That is why the responsible response should be investigation, not trial by social media. KFC Ghana should explain what happened. Not necessarily with a defensive corporate statement. With facts. What level of customer turnout did the company anticipate? What safety plan was prepared? What security arrangements were put in place? What instructions were security personnel given? How many incidents were recorded? Were there injuries? What steps were taken when particular branches became overwhelmed? And most importantly, what is KFC doing to prevent a repeat? The Silence Is Also a Communications Problem As someone who has worked extensively in public relations and crisis communications, I find the communication dimension particularly important. When an organisation’s physical operations generate widespread public concern, silence creates an information vacuum. And information vacuums are quickly filled by everybody else. Customers. Influencers. Newsrooms. Bloggers. Politicians. Commentators. Some will be accurate. Others will not. That is precisely why crisis communication matters. A company does not necessarily have to admit legal liability simply because it communicates after an incident. It can acknowledge what happened, express concern for anyone affected, explain what it knows, confirm that it is investigating and outline immediate corrective measures. That is responsible corporate communication. In my view, silence is rarely a good crisis strategy when the public is asking legitimate questions. The Customer Should Not Carry the Entire Burden There is another uncomfortable part of this conversation. Customers also have responsibilities. Breaking doors, pushing people, attacking staff or refusing lawful instructions cannot be justified simply because a product is being sold cheaply. But we must avoid the opposite mistake of placing the entire burden on consumers. A business designing a high-demand promotion possesses resources, professional expertise and operational control that an individual customer does not. The responsibility is therefore shared, but it is not necessarily equal. Customers must behave responsibly. Companies must plan responsibly. Security personnel must act lawfully. Regulators must regulate. And where harm occurs, the legal system must determine responsibility based on evidence. Ghana Needs to Take Corporate Accountability Seriously This incident should not become another social media controversy that disappears after a few days. It should become a useful case study. Not just for KFC. For every company operating in Ghana. If your campaign can attract thousands of people, crowd safety is part of the campaign. If your event can create congestion, access management is part of the event. If you engage security personnel, their conduct forms part of your operational risk. If something goes wrong, your crisis response becomes part of your corporate responsibility. And if people are injured, the appropriate authorities should establish what happened. That is not anti-business. It is actually pro-business. Strong businesses operate in environments where customers trust them, regulators take their responsibilities seriously and companies understand that commercial decisions have consequences. The Real Question I do not believe the central question should simply be: “Was KFC wrong?” That is too simplistic. The better question is: “What did KFC reasonably know, what risks could it reasonably have anticipated, what precautions did it take, and what happened when those precautions proved inadequate?” Those are questions that evidence can answer. If the evidence establishes negligence, unlawful conduct or regulatory breaches, then the appropriate legal and regulatory consequences should follow. If the evidence does not establish those things, KFC deserves the same fairness we demand for everyone else. That is what accountability should look like. Not outrage. Not mob justice. Not blaming consumers. Not protecting powerful companies. Just evidence, responsibility and the law. By: Philip Nai Philip Nai is a media executive with almost two decades of experience across radio and television production, digital marketing, public relations, brand strategy and strategic communications. He is a Chartered Brand Management Professional and a student of the law. His writings examine issues at the intersection of media, business, brands, communications, public accountability and the law.

items.title: Bittou : Un chef coutumier offre une tronçonneuse et des herbicides aux forces combattantes
items.description: Burkina/Bittou-Don-FDS Bittou : Un chef coutumier offre une tronçonneuse et des herbicides aux forces combattantes Bittou, 16 août 2026 (AIB) – Un natif de Bittou, par ailleurs chef coutumier d’un quartier, a offert, samedi 15 août 2026, une tronçonneuse d’une valeur de plus de 300 000 FCFA ainsi que des herbicides aux Forces de défense et de sécurité (FDS) et aux Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie (VDP), en vue de soutenir leurs actions sur le terrain. Le don a été présenté à l’occasion d’une journée de désherbage organisée par les forces combattantes, en collaboration avec la population de Bittou. L’activité visait notamment à débarrasser les alentours des positions des Forces combattantes des arbres et des herbes susceptibles de réduire leur visibilité. Selon le donateur, ce geste s’inscrit dans une volonté d’encourager les FDS et les VDP engagés dans la lutte pour la reconquête du territoire national. « Il est de mon devoir de soutenir les forces combattantes. C’est parce que le pays est en paix que nous pouvons parler d’activités commerciales et autres », a-t-il déclaré, appelant les populations à apporter leur contribution à l’effort national. Le chef coutumier a également salué la détermination et l’engagement des FDS et des VDP sur le terrain. Il a estimé que le soutien de la population constitue un encouragement important pour les forces combattantes dans l’accomplissement de leur mission. Il a, par ailleurs, invité les habitants de Bittou à maintenir leur accompagnement aux forces combattantes et à participer, selon leurs moyens, aux initiatives contribuant à la reconquête du territoire national. Le garant de la tradition a assuré qu’il demeure engagé aux côtés des autorités et des forces combattantes pour accompagner les actions de développement de la commune et celles liées à la reconquête du territoire. La journée de désherbage a ainsi constitué une occasion pour les forces combattantes et les populations de Bittou de renforcer leur collaboration autour d’une action d’intérêt collectif. Agence d'information du Burkina SK-DNK

items.description: Koulpélogo/Yargatenga : Le tournoi inter-métiers démarre par un match nul Yargatenga, 15 août 2026 (AIB)-Le coup d’envoi de la 3ᵉ édition de la coupe inter-métiers a été donné samedi 15 août 2026 sur le terrain communal de Cinkansé, dans la commune de Yargatenga, sous la présidence du représentant du Président de la délégation spéciale (PDS), en présence du Directeur provincial des Sports, de la Jeunesse et de l’Emploi et des autorités militaires et paramilitaires de la province. Pour ce match d’ouverture, l’équipe des « Serviteurs du peuple » a affronté celle des « Commerçants ». Les deux formations se sont séparées sur un score nul et vierge de 0-0. Au nom du PDS de Yargatenga, Panguiyan Abraham Diessongo a souhaité la bienvenue aux participants et remercié le ministère ainsi que la Direction provinciale des Sports, de la Jeunesse et de l’Emploi pour l’organisation de cette compétition qui réunit les différents corps de métier de la commune. Il s’est également réjoui de la mobilisation des responsables du sport, de la jeunesse et de l’emploi, des entraîneurs, des joueurs, des arbitres et des supporters. Selon M. Diessongo, cette compétition ne vise pas uniquement la pratique sportive et la promotion de la santé. Elle constitue également un cadre de renforcement de la cohésion sociale, de l’union et du vivre-ensemble entre les différents corps de métier. « Il faut vraiment la tolérance. Bonne compétition et que le meilleur gagne », a-t-il déclaré avant de donner officiellement le coup d’envoi du tournoi. Le Directeur provincial des Sports, de la Jeunesse et de l’Emploi par intérim du Koulpélogo, Moustapha Yangané, a rappelé le succès et l’engouement suscités par les deux premières éditions. Pour cette troisième édition, sept équipes sont engagées. Elles disputeront au total 25 matchs sous forme de championnat, sur une période d’environ un mois. La finale est prévue pour le 12 septembre 2026. Moustapha Yangané a invité les joueurs, entraîneurs et supporters à faire preuve de fair-play et à respecter les règles du jeu. « Vous avez vos métiers mais vous vous êtes retrouvés sur le terrain pour communier. Donc, c’est le sport pour tous », a-t-il souligné. Lancé sous de bons auspices, le tournoi inter-métiers de Yargatenga entend ainsi offrir aux travailleurs un espace de détente, de fraternité et de renforcement de la cohésion sociale. Agence d’Information du Burkina LM/bp/yos

items.title: Gourma/Vacances Faso Mêbo 2026 : Le ministre de la Santé encourage les campeurs à devenir des ambassadeurs de la santé
items.description: BURKINA-GOURMA-VACANCES-CAMP-FASO-MEBO Gourma/Vacances Faso Mêbo 2026 : Le ministre de la Santé encourage les campeurs à devenir des ambassadeurs de la santé Fada N’Gourma, 16 août 2026 (AIB)-Le ministre de la Santé, Dr Robert Jean-Claude Lucien Kargougou, à la tête d’une délégation ministérielle, a rendu visite, le dimanche 16 août 2026 à Fada N’Gourma, aux campeurs de l’édition 2026 du camp vacances Faso Mêbo, afin de s’enquérir du déroulement du camp et de les encourager dans les activités patriotiques et citoyennes qu’ils mènent. « Le Président du Faso, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré et le Premier ministre, Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo, nous ont demandé de venir à Fada N’Gourma, de vous saluer, de vous voir et de voir comment votre camp se passe », a déclaré le ministre de la Santé, Dr Robert Jean-Claude Lucien Kargougou. A l’issue de cette visite, le ministre s’est dit satisfait des premiers acquis enregistrés par les campeurs en seulement quelques jours. Il a notamment relevé leur appropriation progressive des valeurs de discipline et d’organisation, ainsi que leur apprentissage dans la confection des pavés et les travaux d’embellissement de la cité. « Nous pouvons aller dire au camarade Président du Faso que les campeurs ont déjà beaucoup appris en seulement quelques jours », a-t-il affirmé. Dr Kargougou a félicité les jeunes et les a exhortés à rester disciplinés et à écouter les conseils des formateurs et des encadreurs. « Le Burkina Faso de demain se construit aujourd’hui à partir d’ici », a-t-il souligné et a invité les campeurs à tirer pleinement profit des enseignements reçus au cours de leur séjour. Le ministre de la Santé a également appelé les jeunes à devenir des ambassadeurs de la santé dans leurs familles, leurs secteurs, leurs villages et leurs communautés. Selon lui, la lutte contre le paludisme, la dengue et les autres maladies transmises par les moustiques passent notamment par l’assainissement du cadre de vie et l’adoption de bonnes pratiques d’hygiène. Il a ainsi exhorté les campeurs à sensibiliser leurs proches sur la nécessité d’éliminer les eaux stagnantes dans les boîtes de conserve, pneus usagés, plats, calebasses, canaris et autres récipients susceptibles de servir de gîtes larvaires aux moustiques. « Quand vous allez rentrer à la maison, dans vos familles, c’est vous qui devez chaque fois dire aux parents : il y a cette boîte de sardines, il y a de l’eau dedans, il faut la renverser », a-t-il expliqué, appelant les jeunes à jouer pleinement leur rôle dans la prévention des maladies. Le ministre Kargougou a, enfin, exprimé sa fierté aux campeurs et les a encouragés à poursuivre leurs efforts avec discipline et engagement. « Nous sommes fiers de vous. Félicitations et bon courage pour la suite de votre camp », a-t-il conclu, avant de reprendre avec les campeurs la devise patriotique : « La Patrie ou la Mort, nous vaincrons ! ». Agence d’information du Burkina KAC/HB/OO

items.title: Paris en ligne : l'essor d'un marché offshore hors contrôle
items.description: Accessible en quelques clics, le marché des paris en ligne s'est imposé au Maroc sans véritable cadre dédié. Les plateformes étrangères y recrutent des joueurs, tandis que le Royaume ne dispose toujours pas d'un système de licences pour encadrer ces activités. Un rapport consacré au marché africain des jeux d'argent en ligne dresse le constat d'un secteur en pleine expansion qui échappe largement à la régulation nationale. Le marché marocain des jeux d'argent connaît une transformation progressive sous l'effet du numérique. Si les activités traditionnelles, telles que les loteries, les paris sportifs, les paris hippiques et les casinos terrestres, évoluent dans un cadre réglementé, l'essor des plateformes de paris en ligne établies à l'étranger ouvre un nouveau front pour les autorités, confrontées à un secteur qui ne relève d'aucun régime national de licences. C'est le constat dressé par le rapport Primer on Africa's Online Gambling Market , publié par SCCG Research, qui consacre un chapitre au Maroc. L'étude souligne que, contrairement à plusieurs autres marchés africains, le Royaume n'a instauré aucun dispositif permettant à des opérateurs privés de jeux d'argent en ligne d'obtenir une autorisation d'exercer sur son territoire. Les plateformes qui ciblent les joueurs marocains opèrent ainsi depuis l'étranger, sans être soumises à une supervision locale. Le rapport rappelle que le marché légal demeure essentiellement structuré autour de trois acteurs. La Marocaine des Jeux et des Sports (MDJS) détient le monopole des paris sportifs et des loteries, tandis que la Société Royale d'Encouragement du Cheval (SOREC) gère les paris hippiques. Les casinos terrestres, quant à eux, sont autorisés dans certaines villes selon un régime spécifique. En revanche, aucun opérateur privé de paris sportifs ou de casino en ligne ne dispose d'une licence marocaine. Un marché difficile à mesurer L'ampleur réelle des paris effectués par les Marocains sur les plateformes étrangères reste difficile à quantifier, faute de statistiques officielles. Le rapport indique toutefois que les autorités évoquent des centaines de millions de dirhams misés chaque année sur des sites offshore. Sur cette base, ses auteurs estiment que le produit brut des jeux généré par cette activité pourrait représenter entre 50 et 100 millions de dollars, voire davantage. Il s'agit toutefois d'une estimation propre au rapport et non d'un chiffre officiel publié par les autorités marocaines. L'étude souligne également que cette activité repose principalement sur les paris sportifs, alimentés notamment par la forte popularité du football européen auprès des joueurs marocains. Les mises sont réalisées via des cartes bancaires ou des services de paiement en ligne, dans un contexte où le taux de pénétration d'Internet et de la téléphonie mobile facilite largement l'accès aux plateformes numériques. Au-delà des flux financiers, le rapport attire l'attention sur les conséquences de l'absence de cadre réglementaire. Les opérateurs étrangers ne relevant pas d'une autorité marocaine, les joueurs disposent de recours limités en cas de litige portant sur un retrait de gains, la fermeture d'un compte ou les conditions d'utilisation d'une plateforme. Les questions liées à la protection des consommateurs, à la prévention de l'addiction, à la vérification de l'âge des utilisateurs ou encore à la transparence des pratiques commerciales demeurent ainsi en dehors du champ d'intervention des autorités nationales. Un cadre juridique hérité d'une autre époque Pour SCCG Research, cette situation s'explique en partie par un décalage entre l'évolution des usages numériques et un cadre juridique conçu avant l'émergence des plateformes de jeux en ligne. Le rapport rappelle que le texte de référence régissant les jeux de hasard au Maroc encadre essentiellement les activités physiques et les monopoles autorisés, sans prévoir de régime spécifique applicable aux opérateurs numériques établis hors du Royaume. L'étude souligne par ailleurs que le recours individuel à des plateformes étrangères n'est pas, en pratique, au cœur de l'action des autorités, ce qui a favorisé le développement d'un marché qualifié de « zone grise ». Les opérateurs offshore demeurent accessibles depuis le Maroc, alors même qu'ils ne disposent d'aucun agrément national. Le rapport relève enfin que les mesures fiscales introduites en 2025 à l'égard des gains provenant de plateformes étrangères constituent le premier signal tangible d'une prise en compte de cette réalité par les pouvoirs publics. Selon ses auteurs, cette évolution pourrait préfigurer, à terme, une réflexion plus large sur la modernisation du cadre juridique des jeux d'argent et sur l'éventuelle mise en place d'un régime de licences pour les opérateurs en ligne. À ce stade, toutefois, aucune réforme en ce sens n'a encore été adoptée et le calendrier d'une éventuelle évolution demeure incertain. The post Paris en ligne : l'essor d'un marché offshore hors contrôle appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Ahafo Minister cuts sod for 24-hour market project in Tano North
items.description: The Ahafo Regional Minister, Mrs Charity Gardiner, has cut the sod for the construction of a 24-hour market project at Duayaw Nkwanta in the Tano North Municipality of the region. Speaking at a ceremony, she explained that the project would create job opportunities, enhance economic activities, and ultimately improve the livelihoods of the people. Mrs Gardiner thanked the Duayaw-Nkwanta Traditional Council for releasing land for the project, and for their support towards the development. The Tano North Municipal Chief Executive, Mr Pius Sampson Opoku, said the market project was just one of the numerous development projects being executed by the government in the municipality. He commended the government for establishing a Fire Service Training School at Duayaw-Nkwanta, which he added had provided an opportunity for the interested youth to acquire employment in the formal sector. The Tano North Municipal Development Planning Officer, Mr Samuel Essuman, explained that the market project contained a creche, clinic, restaurant, fire and police post as well as a banking hall and standard washrooms. Mr Emmanuel Addison Essuman, the Project Manager for Nielz Construction Limited, the contractor executing the project, said that with the cooperation of the people, the project would be completed within 18 months.

items.title: 14 arrested over suspected narcotics cultivation, distribution in Upper East
items.description: The Upper East Regional Police Command has arrested 14 suspects over their alleged involvement in the cultivation, storage and distribution of narcotic drugs at Daliga in the Nabdam District. The arrests were made on Sunday, August 16, during an intelligence-led operation conducted by the Police Intelligence Directorate (PID) in collaboration with the newly established Black Cobra Team. In a statement issued on Monday, August 17, the Police said the operation followed intelligence gathered on suspected narcotics-related activities in the area. The exercise targeted individuals suspected of cultivating, storing and distributing narcotic substances within the district and other parts of the region. The Police identified 13 of the suspects as Alex Nyaaba, Charles Keleg Dombil, Zimi Pandam, Jennifer Ziini, Tobirr Naab, Yinteng James, Tosil Wandabil, Sandanane Peehim, Borimi Nohoo, Curim Teng, Curim Kugri, Nohou Dagobila and Abane Zangbeog. The Police said a search conducted during the operation led to the discovery of a large quantity of suspected narcotic substances concealed in sacks containing millet and maize. Preliminary investigations indicate that suspected Indian hemp was being cultivated alongside food crops, particularly millet and maize. According to the Police, the practice was intended to conceal the illicit farms and make them more difficult for law enforcement officers to detect. Investigators also suspect that the arrested persons formed part of a supply network providing narcotic drugs to peddlers operating in various parts of the Upper East Region. The arrests form part of efforts by the Upper East Regional Police Command to disrupt the cultivation, supply and distribution of illicit drugs in the region. The Police said the involvement of the PID and the Black Cobra Team formed part of an intelligence-driven approach to identifying and dismantling suspected narcotics networks. The suspects remain in Police custody as investigations continue. The Police said the suspects would be put before court to face the full rigours of the law. The Command has meanwhile appealed to the public to provide information that could assist law enforcement agencies in identifying persons involved in the cultivation, trafficking and distribution of narcotic drugs. Editor’s note: The Police statement reportedly says 14 suspects were arrested but provides names for only 13. The discrepancy should be clarified with the Police before publication, if possible.

items.title: Mouhoun/Deuxième anniversaire de la CNAVC : Une célébration sous le signe de l’engagement citoyen
items.description: BURKINA-MOUHOUN-BONDOUKUY-CNAVC-ANNIVERSAIRE Mouhoun/Deuxième anniversaire de la CNAVC : Une célébration sous le signe de l’engagement citoyen Bondoukuy, 15 août 2026 (AIB)-La sous-section de la Coordination nationale des associations de veille citoyenne (CNAVC) de Bondoukuy a célébré, le samedi 15 août 2026, son deuxième anniversaire à travers plusieurs activités à caractère environnemental, social et patriotique, en présence des autorités administratives, coutumières et religieuses, ainsi que de nombreux habitants de la commune. Placée sous le signe de l’engagement citoyen, de la solidarité et du patriotisme, cette célébration a été marquée notamment par des opérations de plantation d’arbres, des actions de soutien aux structures sanitaires et un geste en faveur de la Gendarmerie nationale. Les activités se sont passées sous la houlette responsables de la sous-section, notamment les camarades Tamboé Gédéon et Coulibaly Didier avec la mobilisation des membres du bureau, des militants et des sympathisants de la Coordination nationale des associations de veille citoyenne (CNAVC) de Bondoukuy. Au titre des actions environnementales, les membres de la CNAVC ont mis en terre 50 plants dans l’enceinte du nouveau Centre médical avec antenne chirurgicale (CMA) de Bondoukuy. A travers cette initiative, l’organisation entend contribuer à l’embellissement du site et à l’amélioration du cadre de vie autour de cette infrastructure sanitaire. La maternité du Centre de santé et de promotion sociale (CSPS) de Bondoukuy a également bénéficié d’un don composé de cinq cartons de savons et d’un sac de détergent. Ce geste vise à soutenir le personnel dans le maintien de l’hygiène des locaux et à contribuer à l’amélioration des conditions d’accueil des usagers. La Gendarmerie nationale de Bondoukuy a, pour sa part, accueilli une autre étape de la célébration. Des plants y ont été mis en terre et un mât ainsi qu’un drapeau national ont été remis aux éléments de la gendarmerie. Ce geste se veut une marque d’attachement aux symboles de la République et de reconnaissance à l’endroit des Forces de défense et de sécurité (FDS) et des Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie (VDP), engagés dans la sécurisation du territoire national. Le Président de la délégation spéciale (PDS) de la commune de Bondoukuy, Lazare Bado, a salué l’initiative noble de la CNAVC et porteuse de valeurs citoyennes. Il a appelé les populations à renforcer l’entente, la cohésion sociale, la solidarité et le vivre-ensemble présentés comme des conditions indispensables au développement de la commune. Lazare Bado a également rendu hommage aux FDS et aux VDP pour les efforts consentis au quotidien dans la protection des populations et la défense du territoire national. A travers ces différentes initiatives, la sous-section de la CNAVC de Bondoukuy entend donner un contenu concret à la veille citoyenne, en l’inscrivant également dans des actions en faveur de l’environnement, de la santé, de la solidarité et du patriotisme. Cette deuxième année d’existence aura ainsi été marquée par des actions symboliques destinées à renforcer l’engagement communautaire et la cohésion sociale dans la commune. Agence d’information du Burkina TT/HB/OO

items.title: Lands Minister backs calls for strategic investor to revive VALCO
items.description: The government is considering the involvement of a strategic investor to restore the Volta Aluminium Company (VALCO) to full-scale production, with the Minister for Lands and Natural Resources, Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah, warning that the company’s current operating position is unsustainable. Mr Buah said VALCO had significant industrial potential but was operating well below the capacity of its infrastructure, making fresh investment necessary to rehabilitate the smelter and support Ghana’s ambition of developing an integrated aluminium industry. “It is bleeding, it is bleeding,” the minister said during a policy engagement with the IMANI Centre for Policy and Education in Accra on Thursday, August 13. He subsequently made his position clear on the way forward: “You need to find a strategic investor.” Capacity concerns Mr Buah said VALCO had five potlines, but only a fraction of the facility’s capacity was currently operational. He explained that the government faced competing demands for limited public resources and could not continue providing the level of capital required to rehabilitate and sustain an underperforming state-owned company. He said the priority should be to make VALCO productive and commercially viable rather than maintain its existing ownership structure without addressing its operational challenges. The minister’s comments form part of broader government efforts to reposition Ghana’s minerals sector and increase the value derived from the country’s natural resources. The policy engagement, held in Accra, brought together officials of the Ministry and representatives of agencies under it, including the Minerals Commission, Forestry Commission, Lands Commission and Ghana Geological Survey Authority. The IMANI delegation was led by its Founding President and Chief Executive Officer, Franklin Cudjoe, and included Vice-President for Strategy Selorm Branttie, writer and IMANI associate Kay Codjoe, and IMANI associate Ransford Brobbey. The engagement followed an August 10, 2026 request by IMANI for a fact-finding discussion on the Ministry’s inherited challenges, performance, operational difficulties, reforms and major policy initiatives. Aluminium industry VALCO remains a key component of Ghana’s long-standing plans to develop an integrated aluminium industry based on the country’s bauxite resources. The government’s broader strategy involves linking bauxite mining, processing and downstream manufacturing to retain a greater share of the value generated from the mineral industry within the country. Mr Buah said restoring VALCO’s productive capacity could therefore have implications beyond the company itself, including employment, industrial development and the expansion of Ghana’s aluminium value chain. He also recounted an instance in which prospective visitors seeking to inspect the facility faced resistance from some workers, an experience he said illustrated some of the challenges surrounding efforts to introduce new investment or partnerships. Investor questions The proposal for a strategic investor is, however, likely to raise questions about the structure of any potential arrangement and the extent of the State’s involvement in VALCO. Issues such as the amount of capital to be invested, rehabilitation of the potlines, future production capacity, employment, ownership, local participation and the cost of power will be critical considerations in determining the terms of any partnership. The government will also have to ensure that any arrangement supports its wider objective of developing an integrated aluminium industry rather than simply addressing VALCO’s immediate financial and operational difficulties. VALCO board offers alternative Meanwhile, the Board Chairman of VALCO has requested a meeting with the IMANI team to present alternative proposals for keeping the company operational. According to the report from the engagement, the Board Chairman disputes the characterisation of VALCO’s financial position, arguing that claims about the company’s losses have been overstated. The differing positions set the stage for further discussion over the future of the state-owned smelter, particularly whether the company should pursue a strategic investment arrangement or alternative measures to restore its operations. For now, Mr Buah’s position is that additional investment is necessary if VALCO is to fulfil its potential and contribute meaningfully to Ghana’s aluminium industry.

items.title: Présidentielle en Zambie: Hakainde Hichilema vers un second mandat
items.description: Le chef de l'État sortant prend une nette avance au vu des dépouillements partiels publiés de l'élection présidentielle, le dimanche 16 août 2026 par les autorités électorales. Malgré des revendications prématurées de l'opposition et un climat de tension émaillé d'incidents, Hakainde Hichilema semble bien parti pour l’emporter dès le premier tour. Les résultats globaux sont prévus pour ce lundi 17 août, selon la commission électorale. Vers une confirmation au sommet de l'État pour Hakainde Hichilema? D'après les données communiquées par la commission électorale, le dimanche 16 août 2026, le président zambien sortant devance largement ses concurrents après le décompte effectué dans plus de la moitié des circonscriptions. Avec 1 544 140 suffrages comptabilisés sur 135 des 226 circonscriptions du pays, le dirigeant de 64 ans enregistre 58,87 % des voix. Un score qui, s'il se confirme, lui permettrait de franchir la barre fatidique des 50 % des suffrages exprimés nécessaire pour s'imposer directement sans passer par un second tour. Son opposant direct, Brian Mundubile (55 ans), se retrouve distancé avec 1 030 662 votes sur l'ensemble des 14 prétendants au fauteuil présidentiel. Ce dernier s'était pourtant déclaré vainqueur un peu plus tôt, affirmant s'être imposé au premier tour et assurant que sa formation politique avait également décroché la majorité des sièges au Parlement. À en croire certaines sources, si le vote du jeudi 13 août dernier s'est déroulé dans un calme relatif, la campagne électorale a été assombrie par de vives dénonciations de la part de l'opposition, qui a fait part d'intimidations, d'interpellations, de kidnappings et d'agressions. La journée de vote a également été le théâtre d'un drame près de la capitale Lusaka, où la police a signalé le décès d'un agent électoral de 57 ans à la suite d'une agression par un groupe d'individus dans un township. Neuf personnes ont été interpellées dans le cadre de cette affaire. A l'issue des votes, le dépouillement qui suivait a été perturbé, occasionnant sa suspension, d'environ six heures, décidée par la commission électorale en raison d'actes violents visant les agents électoraux et de la disparition suspecte de bulletins remplis. L'organe électoral n'a pas indiqué si le matériel dérobé avait été récupéré. Cette interruption momentanée a vivement fait réagir les instances internationales. La mission d'observation de la Communauté de développement de l'Afrique australe (SADC), sous la conduite de l'ancien ministre de la Justice du Malawi, Samuel Tembenu, a déploré une décision ayant suscité «de l'incertitude et de l'inquiétude». De son côté, Reinhold Lopatka, à la tête de la délégation des observateurs du Parlement européen, a estimé que cette mesure était «disproportionnée». Face au risque de dérapage, les différentes missions d'observation, à l'image de celle de l'Union européenne, enjoignent l'ensemble des acteurs politiques à la retenue et à l'apaisement en réclamant la fin des déclarations provocatrices, dans l'attente des résultats globaux prévus pour ce lundi. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article Présidentielle en Zambie: Hakainde Hichilema vers un second mandat est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .
